prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- After nearly 150 years in business, the Rocky Mountain News published its final edition Friday, the victim of a bad economy and the Internet generation. The Rocky Mountain News in Denver, Colorado, published its last edition Friday after 150 years. The final front-page headline simply says: "Goodbye, Colorado." "It is with great sadness that we say goodbye to you today. Our time chronicling the life of Denver and Colorado, the nation and the world, is over." The Rocky Mountain News' owner, E.W. Scripps Co., made the announcement to the newsroom at noon Thursday, ending three months of speculation and drama over its fate. The News had been put up for sale in December. The Rocky Mountain News was the latest victim in an era of shutdowns, layoffs and cutbacks plaguing the newspaper industry. "It's in a free fall and nobody knows where the bottom is. It's kind of like water in the toilet swirling around and nobody knows what's left when you're done flushing," media critic Eric Alterman said.  Watch how the economy and Internet are taking a toll on the industry » . Newspapers across the country are under pressure as readership declines, along with advertising revenue, while more and more Americans get their information online. "All newspapers are under great pressure. They'll survive, but they'll survive in different forms, their costs base will have to be dramatically lowered," said Mort Zuckerman, publisher of the New York Daily News, which has the seventh highest circulation in the country. The dramatic decline in advertising dollars in a brutal economy has forced newspapers to cut costs by firing cartoonists, columnists and others, leaving them searching for jobs in a struggling industry. Pia Catton lost her job as arts editor of the New York Sun five months ago, when the newspaper closed. She has taken a short-term job editing a book, but she thinks she may need to look at different careers soon. "There will always be a market for news, you will always need to know immediately what's happening. Will there be a market for newspapers? That's another question," she said. The Rocky Mountain News had more than 200 editorial employees, according to the Columbia Journalism Review's Web site. Rich Boehne, chief executive officer of Scripps, told employees the newspaper was the victim of a terrible economy, an upheaval in the newspaper industry and multimillion-dollar annual losses. "Denver can't support two newspapers any longer," Boehne said. "It's certainly not good news for you, and it's certainly not good news for Denver." The News has been in a joint operating agreement with The Denver Post since 2001, which combined the papers' business operations in an effort to save money, but left the editorial departments separate. The News' closure leaves Denver with one major newspaper, like most American cities. "We've been, sort of, hanging on the edge for so long," said Mel Pompanio, a presentation editor for the paper. "What a huge loss for Colorado today." This week, the San Francisco Chronicle announced it was in danger of being sold or closed if it doesn't stop losing millions. Officials from the Hearst Corp., owners of the Chronicle, said the paper lost $50 million in 2008 and is on pace to lose more this year. "It's difficult. It's hard," Lynn Bartels, a political reporter and 26-year employee for Scripps, said of the News' closing. "I haven't returned any phone calls yet, because I don't need to be reporting and crying at the same time. I've done that enough." Long faces dominated the newsroom in video posted on the paper's Web site. A few sobs could be heard, too, as the announcement of the closing began to sink in among employees. "I could say stupid things like 'I know how you feel.' I don't," Boehne said. "We are just deeply sorry. I hope you will accept that." CNN's Richard Roth contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — After nearly 150 years in business, the Rocky Mountain News published its final edition on Friday, a victim of the troubled economy and the rise of the Internet generation.

The Denver, Colorado, newspaper ended its 150-year run with a simple front-page headline: “Goodbye, Colorado.”

“It is with great sadness that we say goodbye to you today. Our time chronicling the life of Denver and Colorado, the nation and the world, is over.”

The newspaper’s owner, E.W. Scripps Co., announced the closure to the newsroom at noon Thursday, ending three months of speculation and uncertainty over its fate. The News had been put up for sale in December.

The Rocky Mountain News is the latest casualty in an era of closures, layoffs and cutbacks plaguing the newspaper industry.

“It’s in a free fall and nobody knows where the bottom is. It’s kind of like water in the toilet swirling around and nobody knows what’s left when you’re done flushing,” media critic Eric Alterman said.

Watch how the economy and the Internet are taking a toll on the industry »

Newspapers across the country are under mounting pressure as readership and advertising revenue decline, while growing numbers of Americans turn to the Internet for information.

“All newspapers are under great pressure. They’ll survive, but they’ll survive in different forms; their cost base will have to be dramatically lowered,” said Mort Zuckerman, publisher of the New York Daily News, which has the seventh-highest circulation in the country.

The dramatic decline in advertising revenue amid a brutal economy has forced newspapers to reduce costs by laying off cartoonists, columnists and other employees, leaving many to search for work in an already struggling industry.

Pia Catton lost her job as arts editor of the New York Sun five months ago when the newspaper closed. She has since taken a short-term position editing a book, but believes she may soon need to consider a different career.

“There will always be a market for news; you will always need to know immediately what’s happening. Will there be a market for newspapers? That’s another question,” she said.

According to the Columbia Journalism Review’s website, the Rocky Mountain News employed more than 200 editorial staff members.

Rich Boehne, chief executive officer of Scripps, told employees that the newspaper had fallen victim to a dire economy, upheaval within the newspaper industry and multimillion-dollar annual losses.

“Denver can’t support two newspapers any longer,” Boehne said. “It’s certainly not good news for you, and it’s certainly not good news for Denver.”

Since 2001, the News has operated under a joint operating agreement with The Denver Post. The arrangement combined the newspapers’ business operations in an effort to save money while keeping their editorial departments separate.

The News’ closure leaves Denver with one major newspaper, as is the case in most American cities.

“We’ve been, sort of, hanging on the edge for so long,” said Mel Pompanio, a presentation editor for the newspaper. “What a huge loss for Colorado today.”

This week, the San Francisco Chronicle announced that it was at risk of being sold or closed unless it stopped losing millions of dollars. Officials from the Hearst Corp., which owns the Chronicle, said the newspaper lost $50 million in 2008 and was on pace to lose even more this year.

“It’s difficult. It’s hard,” Lynn Bartels, a political reporter and 26-year Scripps employee, said of the News’ closure. “I haven’t returned any phone calls yet, because I don’t need to be reporting and crying at the same time. I’ve done that enough.”

Video posted on the newspaper’s website showed somber expressions throughout the newsroom. A few sobs could also be heard as employees began to absorb the news of the closure.

“I could say stupid things like, ‘I know how you feel.’ I don’t,” Boehne said. “We are just deeply sorry. I hope you will accept that.”

CNN’s Richard Roth contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
After almost a century and a half of publication, Denver’s Rocky Mountain News released its final issue on Friday, brought down by the weak economy and the growing shift toward online news.

Its last front page carried a brief farewell headline: “Goodbye, Colorado.” In a final message to readers, the newspaper expressed its sorrow and said its role documenting Denver, Colorado, the United States and the wider world had come to an end.

E.W. Scripps Co., the paper’s owner, informed newsroom employees at noon on Thursday that publication would cease. The announcement concluded three months of uncertainty that began when the News was offered for sale in December.

The closure was another example of the layoffs, spending reductions and shutdowns affecting newspapers nationwide. Media critic Eric Alterman compared the industry’s decline to a free fall with no visible endpoint, describing it as water circling a toilet bowl before a flush is complete.

Newspapers throughout the United States have been squeezed by shrinking audiences and falling advertising income as increasing numbers of Americans turn to the Internet for information.

Mort Zuckerman, publisher of the New York Daily News—the nation’s seventh-largest newspaper by circulation—said the entire industry was facing intense pressure. He predicted that newspapers would continue to exist, but in altered forms and with substantially lower operating costs.

The severe recession-driven collapse in advertising revenue has prompted publishers to dismiss cartoonists, columnists and other staff members. Those losing their positions have then had to seek employment in an industry already experiencing widespread difficulties.

Pia Catton, formerly the New York Sun’s arts editor, lost her job when that newspaper shut down five months earlier. Although she found temporary work editing a book, she believed she might soon have to consider another profession. Catton said demand for immediate news would always exist, but whether there would continue to be demand for newspapers was less certain.

According to the Columbia Journalism Review’s website, the Rocky Mountain News employed more than 200 people in its editorial department.

Scripps chief executive Rich Boehne told staff members that the publication had been overwhelmed by the disastrous economy, major disruption across the newspaper business and yearly losses amounting to millions of dollars. He said Denver could no longer sustain two newspapers and acknowledged that the outcome was bad both for employees and for the city.

Since 2001, the News and The Denver Post had operated under a joint agreement that merged their business functions to reduce expenses while keeping their newsrooms independent. With the Rocky Mountain News gone, Denver was left with a single major daily paper, as is the case in most U.S. cities.

Mel Pompanio, a presentation editor at the News, said employees had felt for a long time as though the paper was barely holding on. He called its closure an enormous loss for Colorado.

Elsewhere that week, the San Francisco Chronicle warned that it could be sold or closed unless it brought its multimillion-dollar losses under control. Representatives of its owner, Hearst Corp., said the Chronicle lost $50 million in 2008 and was headed toward an even larger deficit in the current year.

Lynn Bartels, a political reporter who had worked for Scripps for 26 years, described the shutdown as painful and difficult. She said she had not yet returned any calls because she did not want to cry while reporting, something she felt she had already done often enough.

A video published on the News’ website showed somber expressions throughout the newsroom. As employees absorbed the announcement, several could also be heard sobbing.

Boehne told the staff he could not honestly claim to understand exactly what they were experiencing. He instead offered the company’s profound apology and said he hoped employees would accept it.

CNN’s Richard Roth contributed to the report.
outputs.L3:
After nearly 150 years in print, the *Rocky Mountain News* published its final edition under the front-page headline “Goodbye, Colorado.” Its owner, E.W. Scripps Co., announced the closure after failing to find a buyer during the three months the Denver newspaper was on the market.

The paper’s closure was another sign of the deepening crisis facing the newspaper industry, which has experienced widespread shutdowns, layoffs, and cost-cutting measures. Declining readership, falling advertising revenue, a weak economy, and the increasing popularity of online news have placed traditional newspapers under severe financial pressure.

Despite these challenges, industry observers believe newspapers will continue to exist, though likely in different and less expensive forms, with greater emphasis on digital publishing. For many displaced newspaper employees, however, the transition may be difficult, and some may need to seek new careers outside traditional journalism.
outputs.L4:
The Rocky Mountain News published its final edition after nearly 150 years, becoming one of the most prominent casualties of the deepening crisis in the American newspaper industry. Its owner, the E.W. Scripps Company, decided to close the Denver paper after failing to find a buyer willing to take on its mounting financial losses.

Founded in 1859, the Rocky Mountain News had long been an important part of Colorado’s civic and cultural life. Yet its history and loyal readership were not enough to protect it from the forces transforming the media business. Circulation had declined as more readers turned to free online sources, while advertising revenue—traditionally the financial foundation of newspapers—fell sharply. The recession accelerated those losses as businesses reduced spending on classified and display advertising.

The closure left hundreds of journalists and other employees without jobs and Denver with one fewer major daily newspaper. In its final edition, the staff reflected on the paper’s history, celebrated its reporting and said goodbye to readers. The end was especially painful because it came only weeks before the publication would have marked its 150th anniversary.

The Rocky Mountain News was not alone. Newspapers across the United States were cutting staff, reducing the size or frequency of their print editions, closing bureaus and eliminating sections. Some publications entered bankruptcy proceedings, while others shifted resources away from print in an effort to build sustainable online operations. Even once-profitable metropolitan papers found themselves under severe pressure as readers’ habits and advertisers’ priorities changed.

The industry’s difficulties stem from more than the economic downturn. The internet has permanently altered how news is distributed and consumed. Readers increasingly expect immediate access to information, often without paying for it, while digital platforms and classified-advertising websites have captured much of the revenue that once flowed to newspapers. Online advertising has generally failed to generate enough money to support the large staffs and production costs associated with traditional print organizations.

The demise of the Rocky Mountain News therefore served as both a warning and a symbol. Newspapers that survive will probably have to operate with smaller staffs, lower costs and a stronger focus on digital publishing. They will also need to experiment with subscriptions, memberships, targeted advertising and other sources of revenue.

Although the demand for reliable reporting remains strong, the business model that supported newspapers for generations is rapidly disappearing. The challenge for the remaining publications is to preserve serious journalism while adapting to a leaner, faster and increasingly digital future.
